paper.title_en: A Perspective on Topological Charge Density Wave Materials
paper.abstract_en: Charge density waves are among the earliest known ordered states in quantum materials, yet they have re-emerged at the center of modern discussions of topology, symmetry breaking, and collective dynamics. In several material classes, charge-density-wave order reshapes electronic bands, boundary states, defect structures, and electromagnetic responses in ways that invite a topological interpretation. Real-space imaging has shown that incommensurate order can form networks of phase defects rather than uniform modulations. Boundary-resolved spectroscopy has revealed in-gap modes whose existence and spatial structure track the charge-density-wave order, although such observations remain confined to a single material family. In Weyl materials, density-wave gaps have been linked to axion-like magnetoelectric response, placing the charge-density-wave phase within a dynamical-field description of the effective action. In kagome metals, charge order is intertwined with Berry curvature, unconventional symmetry breaking, and superconductivity. These developments have led to the term "topological charge density wave," but the phrase describes several physically distinct phenomena. We distinguish three meanings: (i) topology of the order parameter and its defects, (ii) topology of the charge-density-wave-reconstructed electronic structure and its boundary modes, and (iii) axion-like electromagnetic response generated by density-wave order. The experimental and theoretical support for these three meanings differs substantially. This Perspective traces the development of these ideas, clarifies the evidence behind each class, identifies unresolved questions and points of debate, and outlines experimental criteria for establishing topology in charge-density-wave states.
